project.title: SnapLink: URL Shortener with Analytics and AI Insights
project.tagline: Build a production-style URL shortener from requirements to monitoring, with AI as your pair programmer
project.description: Over nine phases you build SnapLink like a professional team: requirements, design, a test-first implementation, CI/CD with GitHub Actions, Docker, optional free-tier deployment, observability and a retrospective. Pick Java, Python or TypeScript; the spec, database and tests are shared. Everything runs on your laptop, and the AI feature works offline.

One of: Java, Python or TypeScript fundamentals

outcomes: Turn a brief into testable requirements and user stories
Design a REST API contract-first (OpenAPI) with a PostgreSQL schema and ADRs
Implement test-first against a pending test suite, with a Redis cache that degrades gracefully
Build CI/CD with GitHub Actions: matrix, caching, reusable workflows, service containers, GHCR
Containerise with multi-stage Dockerfiles and run the stack with Docker Compose
Add request IDs, JSON logs and metrics, run a game day and write a blameless post-mortem
Use AI assistants deliberately and verify every output
project.ai_feature: AI insights for a link's traffic: offline template by default, optional Ollama or a free Gemini/Groq key
project.portfolio_blurb: Built SnapLink, a URL shortener with click analytics and AI insights: contract-first API, PostgreSQL + Redis with graceful degradation, ≥85 % test coverage, GitHub Actions CI/CD to GHCR, Docker, JSON logs, metrics and a game-day post-mortem.

phases.title: Setup and orientation
phases.heading: Phase 0 · Setup and orientation
phases.why_md:
Every professional project starts with a working local environment and a clean Git workflow. Teams
lose days to "works on my machine". In this phase you set up the tools for **one** track, run the
starter, open your first pull request and start your `AI_LOG.md`. That is the evidence a reviewer
looks for first: a repo that builds from a clean checkout with one command.
objectives: Fork the repository **with all branches and tags**, clone it and add the `upstream` remote.
Pick a track (Java, Python or TypeScript) and install its toolchain on Windows (WSL2), macOS or Linux.
Start PostgreSQL + Redis with Docker Compose and run the starter so `GET /health` returns `UP`.
Run lint and tests locally and see which tests are *pending* and why.
Open a pull request that passes CI and write your first `AI_LOG.md` entry.

steps.title: Fork and clone (keep the tags!)
steps.content_md:
1. On GitHub open `AICanCode-org/snaplink` → **Fork**. **Untick "Copy the `main` branch only"**. The
   `solution` branch and the `phase-N-end` tags are your safety net in later phases.
2. Clone **your** fork and connect the original as `upstream`:
   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/<you>/snaplink.git
   cd snaplink
   git remote add upstream https://github.com/AICanCode-org/snaplink.git
   git fetch upstream --tags
   git tag -l 'phase-*'      # you should see phase-0-end … phase-8-end
   ```
3. **Windows:** do all of this inside **WSL2** (Ubuntu) and keep the repo in the Linux file system
   (`~/code/snaplink`), not under `/mnt/c`. File watching and Docker volumes are 5–10× faster there.

steps.title: Run the checks and meet the pending tests
steps.content_md:
```bash
make lint test
```
You will see **one passing test** (`/health`) and dozens of **skipped** ones. They are *pending*: the
complete test suite for SnapLink is already written and switched off in one file per track:

| Track | Pending list |
|---|---|
| Java | `tracks/java/src/test/java/org/aicancode/snaplink/support/Pending.java` |
| Python | `tracks/python/tests/conftest.py` (`PENDING`) |
| TypeScript | `tracks/typescript/test/pending.ts` (`PENDING`) |

In Phase 3 you delete one line at a time, watch the tests go red, and make them green.

steps.title: Your first pull request
steps.content_md:
1. Create a branch: `git switch -c chore/phase-0-setup`.
2. Fill in the first entry in `AI_LOG.md`, e.g. how an assistant helped you install the toolchain and
   how you checked its advice.
3. Commit and push, then open a PR **in your fork** against your `main`:
   ```bash
   git add AI_LOG.md
   git commit -m "docs: start AI_LOG for phase 0"
   git push -u origin chore/phase-0-setup
   ```
4. Open the **Actions** tab: the CI workflow runs lint + unit tests for all three tracks. Wait for green,
   fill in the PR template and merge.

quiz.q: Why must you untick "Copy the main branch only" when forking?
options: Otherwise GitHub Actions is disabled in the fork
Otherwise the `solution` branch and phase tags are missing from your fork
Otherwise you cannot open pull requests
Otherwise Docker Compose cannot find the database
quiz.explanation: Forks copy only `main` by default. The tags (`phase-N-end`) live on the `solution` branch; without them you cannot compare your work or catch up. Fix it later with `git fetch upstream --tags`.

quiz.q: On Windows, where should the repository live?
options: Inside the WSL2 Linux file system, e.g. `~/code/snaplink`
On a network drive so Docker can share it
quiz.explanation: Cross-file-system access from WSL to `/mnt/c` is slow and breaks file watching. Keep code in the Linux file system and open it with VS Code's WSL extension.

quiz.q: `/health` says `"cache":"DOWN"` but `"status":"UP"`. What does that mean?
options: The app is broken and should be restarted
Redis is unavailable, but the app can still serve requests from PostgreSQL
The health endpoint has a bug
quiz.explanation: Redis is an optional cache (NFR-2). Only the database is required for `UP`; without it the endpoint returns `503`.

quiz.q: Why are most tests skipped in the starter?
options: CI is too slow to run them
They describe behaviour you will implement in Phase 3–4 and are switched on one milestone at a time
They only run on the solution branch
quiz.explanation: The full suite is written up-front (a test-first workflow). Deleting a line from the pending list turns a group back on, so you always have a clear red → green target.

quiz.q: Which of these should never go into an AI prompt?
options: A stack trace from your own code
The contents of your `.env` file with API keys
quiz.explanation: Secrets and personal data never go into prompts. Redact keys before you paste anything.

phases.title: Requirements and user stories
phases.heading: Phase 1 · Requirements and user stories
phases.why_md:
Most failed projects fail before the first line of code: nobody wrote down what "done" means. A short,
testable requirements document lets you say *no* to scope creep, gives every test a reason to exist,
and is the first thing an interviewer asks about ("what were the constraints?"). AI assistants are
great at drafting requirements, and just as good at inventing requirements nobody asked for. Your
job is to keep the ones you can test.
objectives: Turn a one-paragraph brief into numbered **functional** (FR) and **measurable non-functional** (NFR) requirements.
Write 6–8 **user stories** with Given/When/Then acceptance criteria and create them as GitHub Issues.
Write an explicit **out-of-scope** list.
Do a **back-of-the-envelope estimate** (traffic, storage, collision probability) and use it to justify the design.

steps.title: Read the brief and the contract
steps.content_md:
> *Build SnapLink: a self-hostable URL shortener. Users create short links (random or custom alias,
> optional expiry), visitors are redirected, owners see daily click counts and a short weekly insight.
> It must run on a laptop for free, keep working when the cache is down, and store no personal data.*

Open `spec/openapi.yaml`. The HTTP contract is **given** so the three tracks stay compatible; your
requirements must be consistent with it (status codes, limits, error format).

steps.title: Functional requirements
steps.content_md:
In `spec/requirements.md` write FR-1 … FR-n as "The system shall …" statements. Each needs a number
(1–365 days, 2048 characters, 3–32 alias characters) or a status code, so a test can check it.
Bad: *"Links should be short."* Good: *"Codes are 7 Base62 characters."*

steps.title: Non-functional requirements
steps.content_md:
Cover performance, availability, security, privacy, cost and portability. Make each one measurable:
*"p95 redirect latency < 50 ms with a warm cache"*, *"redirects keep working when Redis is down"*,
*"no IP addresses are stored"*.

steps.title: User stories → GitHub Issues
steps.content_md:
For each story use the **User story** issue template (`.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/user_story.yml`). It asks
for the story, the acceptance criteria and the Phase 3 milestone. Label them `user-story`. With the
GitHub CLI:
```bash
gh issue create --template user_story.yml      # or use the web UI: Issues → New issue
```

steps.title: Out of scope + estimates
steps.content_md:
List what v1 will **not** do (accounts, UI dashboard, QR codes, rate limiting…). Then estimate:
links/day, read:write ratio, requests/second at peak (× 10 of average), storage per year, and the
chance that a random 7-character code collides. Write one sentence on what the numbers mean for the design.

steps.title: Commit
steps.content_md:
```bash
git switch -c docs/phase-1-requirements
git add spec/requirements.md AI_LOG.md
git commit -m "docs(spec): requirements, user stories and estimates"
git push -u origin docs/phase-1-requirements     # open a PR, merge when CI is green
```
The track code does not change in this phase, so `make lint test` behaves exactly as in Phase 0.

ai_prompts.title: Draft requirements from the brief
ai_prompts.prompt:
Act as a senior engineer. From this brief, write numbered functional requirements (FR-n, "The system
shall ...") and measurable non-functional requirements (NFR-n) for a URL shortener. Every requirement
must be testable: include numbers, limits or HTTP status codes. Stay consistent with this OpenAPI
contract: <paste the paths + schemas of spec/openapi.yaml>. Brief: <paste>. Do NOT add features that
are not in the brief; list anything you were tempted to add under "Out of scope".
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: checking every FR against `spec/openapi.yaml` (same limits, same status codes), deleting anything you cannot write a test for, and moving invented features (accounts, QR codes, analytics by country) to *Out of scope*.

ai_prompts.title: Acceptance criteria review
ai_prompts.prompt:
Here are my user stories with acceptance criteria: <paste>. For each story, list (a) criteria that are
ambiguous or not testable, (b) a missing edge case, (c) the HTTP request + expected response that
would prove the criterion. Answer as a table.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: turning at least two of the suggested request/response pairs into `curl` commands you will run in Phase 3, and rejecting edge cases that contradict the contract.

ai_prompts.title: Check my estimate
ai_prompts.prompt:
I estimate 1,000 new links/day and a 100:1 read:write ratio. Check my arithmetic for average and peak
requests per second, yearly storage at 0.5 KB per row, and the probability that a new random
7-character Base62 code collides when 1 million codes exist. Show each calculation step.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: redoing the arithmetic yourself (62⁷ ≈ 3.52 × 10¹²; 100,000 / 86,400 ≈ 1.16 req/s). LLMs make arithmetic slips; a calculator does not.

deliverables.text: `spec/requirements.md` with FRs, measurable NFRs, ≥ 6 user stories with acceptance criteria, out of scope, estimates.
One GitHub Issue per user story, labelled `user-story`, each assigned to a Phase 3 milestone.
An `AI_LOG.md` entry that records at least one AI suggestion you **rejected** and why.
Compare with the reference: `git diff phase-0-end phase-1-end -- spec/requirements.md`.

quiz.q: Which requirement is testable?
options: "p95 server-side redirect latency is below 50 ms with a warm cache."
quiz.explanation: Only the third one has a measurable threshold and a condition. The others need numbers before they can be tested.

quiz.q: Why does SnapLink use `302` instead of `301` (and why is that a requirement, not just a detail)?
options: Browsers cache `301` permanently, which would break expiry, deletion and click counting
quiz.explanation: FR-3, FR-5 and FR-6 only work if every click reaches the server. That constraint leads to ADR-0002 in Phase 2.

quiz.q: With 1 million existing random 7-character Base62 codes, the chance that a new code collides is about…
options: Zero, codes are unique by construction
quiz.explanation: 10⁶ / 62⁷ ≈ 10⁶ / 3.5 × 10¹² ≈ 2.8 × 10⁻⁷. That is rare, but not zero, so the database must still enforce uniqueness and the app retries.

quiz.q: What belongs in "Out of scope"?
options: Features you deliberately will not build in this version, so reviewers know it was a decision
quiz.explanation: Writing the list down stops scope creep and shows judgement. "No accounts in v1" is a decision, not an omission.

quiz.q: "Redirects keep working when Redis is down" is an example of…
options: An availability NFR that will become an integration test
An implementation detail you should not write down
quiz.explanation: It is about *how well* the system behaves under failure. Phase 4 proves it with a test that points the cache at a dead port.

recap: How to turn a fuzzy brief into numbered, testable FRs and measurable NFRs.

Back-of-the-envelope estimation and how it justifies (or rules out) complexity.
Using AI to draft, and your own judgement and arithmetic to verify.

phases.title: Design (architecture, DB schema, API contract)
phases.heading: Phase 2 · Design: architecture, database schema, API contract
phases.why_md:
Design is where you make the expensive decisions on purpose: how codes are generated, what is cached,
where the source of truth lives, what happens when something fails. Writing them down as diagrams
and **Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)** lets a reviewer follow your reasoning in minutes, and
lets future-you remember *why*. The SQL schema is the one artefact that is shared by all three
tracks, so a mistake here costs three times.
objectives: Draw context, container and sequence diagrams in Mermaid (rendered by GitHub).
Write three ADRs: short-code generation, redirect status code, click counting.
Design the PostgreSQL schema and write it as migration `spec/db/migrations/V1__init.sql`.
Read the given OpenAPI contract and map each endpoint to a requirement.
Watch your track's migrator apply V1 on start-up.

steps.title: Diagrams in `spec/architecture.md`
steps.content_md:
Mermaid is text, so it diffs and reviews like code. Start with a container diagram:
```text
flowchart TB
    client([HTTP clients]) --> app["SnapLink app :8080"]
    app -- "SQL (source of truth)" --> pg[("PostgreSQL")]
    app -- "cache-aside, 500 ms timeout" --> redis[("Redis")]
    app -. "optional, falls back to template" .-> llm[("LLM endpoint")]
```
Wrap it in a code fence with the language `mermaid` and preview it on GitHub or in VS Code (extension
"Markdown Preview Mermaid Support"). Then draw the **redirect sequence**: cache hit, cache miss,
unknown code, expired link, and Redis down.

steps.title: ADRs
steps.content_md:
Copy `spec/adr/0000-template.md` three times:
1. `0001-short-code-generation.md`: sequence + Base62 vs hash vs random CSPRNG + retry. Use your Phase 1 collision estimate.
2. `0002-302-redirects.md`: `301` vs `302` vs `307`, and what browser caching does to analytics.
3. `0003-click-counting.md`: two statements vs one atomic statement vs Redis `INCR` + periodic flush.

Each ADR is one page: context, options with pros/cons, decision, consequences.

steps.title: Schema → `spec/db/migrations/V1__init.sql`
steps.content_md:
Requirements to satisfy:
- `links`: surrogate `BIGSERIAL` id, unique `code` (≤ 32 chars), `long_url` ≤ 2048 enforced by a
  `CHECK`, `is_custom`, `created_at`, nullable `expires_at`, `click_count`.
- A **partial index** on `expires_at` for rows that can expire.
- `click_daily(link_id, day, clicks)` with a composite primary key and `ON DELETE CASCADE`.

Name the unique constraint (`uq_links_code`) so that error messages and tests can refer to it. Never
edit a migration after it is merged. Add `V2__…` instead (you will do that in Phase 7).

steps.title: Watch the migrator apply it
steps.content_md:
Every track runs the same tiny migrator at start-up (≈ 40 lines, no Flyway/Alembic, so the three tracks
can share one SQL file). Start your app (`make run`) and inspect the result:
```bash
docker compose exec postgres psql -U snaplink -d snaplink -c '\d links' -c 'select * from schema_migrations'
```

quiz.q: Why is uniqueness of `code` enforced by a database constraint instead of "SELECT first, then INSERT"?
options: Two concurrent requests can both see "free" and both insert. Only the constraint is race-free
quiz.explanation: Check-then-act is a race. Insert, catch the unique violation, and retry (random code) or return `409` (custom alias).

quiz.q: What does the partial index `… WHERE expires_at IS NOT NULL` buy us?
options: An index only over rows that can expire, so it stays small
It speeds up redirects by code
quiz.explanation: Most links never expire; indexing only the others keeps the index small for future clean-up jobs.

quiz.q: Why does `click_daily` reference `links(id)` with `ON DELETE CASCADE`?
options: Deleting a link must delete its analytics too (FR-6), without extra application code
Postgres requires it for composite keys
quiz.explanation: The database guarantees there are no orphan rows. The app still has to evict the cache entry itself.

quiz.q: Why do all three tracks use a hand-written migrator instead of Flyway / Alembic / node-pg-migrate?
options: One set of plain SQL files is shared by all tracks; a 40-line migrator behaves identically in each
quiz.explanation: It is a teaching trade-off: one schema, three languages. In a single-language team you would normally pick the ecosystem's tool.

quiz.q: Which statement about an ADR is true?
options: It is written after the code, to document what was built
It records the context, the options considered and the consequences of one decision
It must be approved by a manager
quiz.explanation: ADRs are short and specific. When a decision changes, a new ADR *supersedes* the old one rather than editing history.

M2: create, get, delete, redirect (US-1, US-3, US-4, US-6)
steps.content_md:
Un-pend **service** and **api**. Some of their tests belong to M3/M4/M5 and stay red for now; that is
expected. Implement `create`, `get`, `delete`, `resolve` in the service and `insert`, `findByCode`,
`delete` in the Postgres repository.
- Random codes: insert, and on a duplicate-key error retry (max 5). Custom alias: duplicate → `409`.
- `resolve`: unknown → `404`, expired → `410`, otherwise return the long URL. The route sends `302`
  with `Cache-Control: no-store` (ADR-0002).
- Use the injected **clock**, never "now" directly. That is how the tests travel in time.

Try it against the real database:
```bash
docker compose up -d postgres redis && make run      # in tracks/<track>
curl -si -X POST localhost:8080/api/v1/links -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
     -d '{"url":"https://www.aicancode.org","alias":"acc","expiresInDays":7}'
curl -si localhost:8080/acc            # 302, Location: https://www.aicancode.org
```

steps.title: M3: cache-aside + click counting (US-4, NFR-2)
steps.content_md:
Implement the Redis cache (`get`/`put`/`delete`, key `snaplink:link:{code}`, JSON `{id,url,expiresAt}`)
and the click counter. Rules:
- TTL = `min(3600, seconds until expiry)`. A cached entry must **never** outlive the link.
- Check expiry **after** the cache lookup too: an entry cached yesterday can be expired today.
- Every Redis error is logged and treated as a miss. Redis is optional.
- Count the click with **one** SQL statement (ADR-0003). A failure is logged, the redirect still succeeds.

```sql
WITH bumped AS (
    UPDATE links SET click_count = click_count + 1 WHERE id = $1 RETURNING id
)
INSERT INTO click_daily (link_id, day, clicks)
SELECT id, $2, 1 FROM bumped
ON CONFLICT (link_id, day) DO UPDATE SET clicks = click_daily.clicks + 1;
```
Check it: `docker compose exec redis redis-cli keys 'snaplink:*'` after a redirect, then
`docker compose stop redis` and redirect again. It must still work (`/health` shows `cache: DOWN`).

steps.title: M4: stats (US-5)
steps.content_md:
`GET /api/v1/links/{code}/stats?days=7` returns one entry per **UTC** day, oldest first, **zero-filled**
(the table only has rows for days with clicks). Implement `dailyClicks` in the repository and
`stats`/`dailySeries` in the service.

steps.title: M5: AI insights with an offline fallback (US-8)
steps.content_md:
Un-pend **insights**. Three pieces:
1. `TemplateInsightGenerator`: deterministic and offline. The wording is part of the spec (identical in
   all tracks), e.g. `/acc got 3 clicks in the last 7 days (all-time: 3). Busiest day: 2026-10-02 with 3
   clicks. Trend: up compared with earlier in the week.` Busiest day: earliest wins ties. Trend: sum of
   the last ⌊n/2⌋ days vs the first ⌊n/2⌋.
2. `LlmInsightGenerator`: one `POST {LLM_BASE_URL}/chat/completions` (the OpenAI-compatible format that
   Ollama, Gemini and Groq all accept), with a timeout.
3. `InsightService`: use the LLM if configured; on **any** error, return the template text with
   `fallback: true`.

Run it three ways:
```bash
make run                                                     # template (default, offline)
INSIGHTS_PROVIDER=llm LLM_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:9/v1 make run   # unreachable → fallback: true
# Optional, local and free:  docker compose --profile ollama up -d
#   docker compose exec ollama ollama pull llama3.2:1b
#   INSIGHTS_PROVIDER=llm LLM_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1 make run
curl -s localhost:8080/api/v1/links/acc/insights
```
A free Gemini or Groq key also works (`LLM_BASE_URL`, `LLM_MODEL`, `LLM_API_KEY` in `.env.example`).
Keep the key in your shell or `.env`, never in Git.

steps.title: Review the AI's code (exercise)
steps.content_md:
An assistant produced this `resolve` (pseudo-code). Find the bug **before** reading on, then write the
failing test.
```text
cached = cache.get(code) or repo.find(code)
repo.recordClick(cached.id, today)
if cached.expired(now): raise Gone
return cached.url
```
The click is counted **before** the expiry check, so expired links still gain clicks, and if the
cache path skips the check entirely, expired links redirect for up to an hour. The unit suite catches
both: the *"expired link is 410 even when cached"* test checks the status, that the cache entry was
evicted, and that the expired attempt did not add a click. Note in `AI_LOG.md` how you found it.

quiz.q: Why must the service use an injected clock?
options: It is faster than the system clock
Tests can move time forward to check expiry without sleeping
quiz.explanation: `clock.advance(days=2)` makes "expired" deterministic. Code that calls `now()` directly can only be tested by waiting.

quiz.q: A link expires in 10 minutes. What TTL should its cache entry get?
options: 600 seconds: never longer than the time left until expiry
quiz.explanation: `min(3600, seconds until expiry)`. The service also re-checks expiry on every hit, as a second line of defence.

quiz.q: Redis times out during a redirect. What should happen?
options: Log a warning, treat it as a cache miss and serve from PostgreSQL
Return 302 to a cached default page
quiz.explanation: The cache is an optimisation (NFR-2). Short timeouts (500 ms) keep a dead Redis from slowing every request.

quiz.q: Why is a random code inserted and retried on a duplicate-key error instead of checked first?
options: Checking is not possible in SQL
Check-then-insert races; the unique constraint is the only reliable judge
The tests require exactly five database calls
quiz.explanation: See ADR-0001. Custom aliases are *not* retried: a duplicate alias is the user's problem (`409`).

quiz.q: What must `/insights` return when the LLM endpoint is unreachable?
options: `200` with the template summary, `provider: "template"` and `fallback: true`
quiz.explanation: The AI feature is a nice-to-have on top of a deterministic baseline. Users always get an answer, and `fallback` makes the degradation visible.

quiz.q: In the AI-generated `resolve`, what is the bug?
options: It records the click before checking expiry, so expired links gain clicks (and may still redirect from the cache)
It raises an exception for expired links
quiz.explanation: Order matters: look up → check expiry (evict if expired) → count → redirect. A test caught it, not a code review.

recap: Test-first development with a pending list: red → green → refactor, one milestone at a time.
A layered design: thin HTTP layer, framework-free service, repository and cache ports with real and in-memory adapters.
Cache-aside with TTLs bounded by business rules, and graceful degradation when the cache fails.
Atomic counters in one SQL statement.
Integrating an LLM behind an interface with a timeout and a deterministic fallback.
Reviewing AI-generated code with tests instead of trust.

phases.title: Testing (unit, integration, contract, coverage)
phases.heading: Phase 4 · Testing: integration tests, failure tests and a coverage gate
phases.why_md:
Unit tests with in-memory fakes prove your logic. They cannot prove that your SQL is valid, that the
unique constraint really fires, that `ON DELETE CASCADE` works or that the app survives a dead Redis.
Integration tests against **real** PostgreSQL and Redis do. A coverage gate then stops the suite from
quietly rotting. Together they let you change code (or accept an AI's refactor) without fear.
objectives: Explain the test pyramid for SnapLink: unit (fast, many), integration (real dependencies), smoke/contract (black-box, few).
Run the integration suite against the Compose services using a **separate** test database.
Prove failure behaviour: Redis down, an expiry stored in the database, cascading deletes.
Enforce ≥ 85 % line coverage locally and understand what the number does and does not mean.

steps.title: Know the layers you already have
steps.content_md:
| Layer | Where | Needs | Run |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unit | `…/unit/…`, in-memory repo + cache, fake clock | nothing | `make test` |
| Integration | `…/integration/…`, real Postgres + Redis | `docker compose up -d postgres redis` | `make test-integration` |
| Smoke (black-box) | `scripts/smoke-test.sh` (Phase 6) | a running app | `scripts/smoke-test.sh` |

The integration tests use `TEST_DATABASE_URL` (default `…/snaplink_test`) and `TEST_REDIS_URL`
(default `redis://localhost:6379/1`), so they **truncate test data, never your dev data**.

phases.title: CI with GitHub Actions
phases.heading: Phase 5 · Continuous integration with GitHub Actions
phases.why_md:
"It passed on my machine" is not evidence. CI runs the same checks on a clean machine for every push
and pull request, so a broken change never reaches `main`. It is also the cheapest code reviewer you
will ever have. In this phase you grow the starter workflow into a real pipeline: path filters, a
reusable workflow, service containers for integration tests, caching, a coverage artefact and one
required status check.

Every keyword used here is explained slowly in **[docs/github-actions-explained.md](github-actions-explained.md)**.
Read it side by side with the YAML.
objectives: Explain triggers, jobs, steps, runners, `needs`, `if`, matrices, caching and artefacts.
Write a **reusable workflow** (`workflow_call`) that runs one track's full check, and call it three times.
Run integration tests in CI with PostgreSQL + Redis **service containers**.
Skip unaffected tracks with a **path filter**, and still have a single required check (`ci-ok`).
Validate the OpenAPI contract in CI and enable **Dependabot**.
Protect `main` so a PR cannot be merged while CI is red.

steps.title: Read the starter workflow
steps.content_md:
Open `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. It is a **matrix** over `[java, python, typescript]`; each matrix job
sets up one toolchain (`if: matrix.track == 'java'`), then runs `make install`, `make lint` and `make test`.
The same Makefile targets exist in every track, so CI does not need three different scripts.

steps.title: Create the reusable workflow
steps.content_md:
Create `.github/workflows/reusable-track-ci.yml` with `on: workflow_call` and an input `track`. Give its job:
- `services:` `postgres:16-alpine` and `redis:7-alpine` with health checks and published ports,
- `env:` `TEST_DATABASE_URL` / `TEST_REDIS_URL` pointing at `localhost`,
- the setup steps from the starter, then `make install lint test`,
- a step that creates `snaplink_test` (`docker exec ${{ job.services.postgres.id }} psql …`),
- `make coverage` (unit + integration + the 85 % gate),
- `actions/upload-artifact@v4` for the coverage report (`if: always()`).

steps.title: Rewrite `ci.yml` as an orchestrator
steps.content_md:
1. A `changes` job with `dorny/paths-filter@v3` that outputs `shared`, `java`, `python`, `typescript`.
2. A `contract` job (only when shared files change): `pipx run openapi-spec-validator spec/openapi.yaml`
   and `shellcheck` on `scripts/*.sh`.
3. Three jobs `java`, `python`, `typescript`, each `uses: ./.github/workflows/reusable-track-ci.yml`
   with `if:` on its path output.
4. A final `ci-ok` job with `if: always()` and `needs:` on all of them that fails when any result is
   `failure` or `cancelled`. Skipped is fine.

The reference is at `git show phase-5-end:.github/workflows/ci.yml`.

steps.title: Lint your workflows before pushing
steps.content_md:
```bash
# https://github.com/rhysd/actionlint  (Go binary; also available via Homebrew / Docker)
go install github.com/rhysd/actionlint/cmd/actionlint@latest
actionlint                       # run from the repo root
```
`actionlint` catches typos in expressions, unknown inputs, bad `needs` and shell bugs (via shellcheck)
before GitHub ever sees them.

steps.title: Dependabot
steps.content_md:
Add `.github/dependabot.yml` with one entry per ecosystem: `maven` in `/tracks/java`, `pip` in
`/tracks/python`, `npm` in `/tracks/typescript`, and `github-actions` in `/`. Group minor + patch updates
so you get one PR per ecosystem per week.

steps.title: Protect `main`
steps.content_md:
In your fork: **Settings → Branches → Add branch ruleset** (or classic rule) for `main`:
- Require a pull request before merging.
- Require status checks to pass → add **`ci-ok`** (it appears after the first run).
- Block force pushes.

Because skipped jobs count as success, a docs-only PR still gets a green `ci-ok` quickly.

steps.title: Prove it works
steps.content_md:
Open a PR that breaks one test in **one** track: only that track's job runs (path filter) and `ci-ok`
goes red, so the merge button is blocked. Fix it and watch it go green. Then open a PR that only touches
`spec/openapi.yaml`: all jobs run, because a contract change affects every track.

quiz.q: What does `on: workflow_call` mean?
options: The workflow runs when someone calls the repository's API
The workflow can be used as a reusable workflow by other workflows (`jobs.<id>.uses`)
The workflow runs on every push
The workflow can only be run manually
quiz.explanation: A reusable workflow is like a function: it declares `inputs`, and the caller passes them with `with:`.

quiz.q: Why is `ci-ok` the only required check instead of every job?
options: GitHub allows only one required check
With path filters some jobs are skipped; one aggregator job gives a stable name that is green when nothing failed
Reusable workflows cannot be required checks
quiz.explanation: Required checks are matched by name. An aggregator with `if: always()` survives jobs being skipped or renamed.

quiz.q: How do integration tests reach PostgreSQL in CI?
options: They connect to a free cloud database
A `services:` container runs next to the job and its port is published on `localhost`
Docker Compose is started inside the test
quiz.explanation: Service containers live for one job, are health-checked before steps start, and are thrown away afterwards.

quiz.q: What does `cache: npm` (or `maven`/`pip`) in a setup action do?
options: Restores the package download cache keyed by a hash of the lock file, so installs are faster
quiz.explanation: The key changes when `package-lock.json` / `pom.xml` / `requirements-dev.txt` changes, so you never get stale dependencies.

quiz.q: Which default `permissions` block is safest for a CI workflow that only reads code?
quiz.explanation: Least privilege. Jobs that need more (e.g. pushing images) ask for it explicitly, as `deploy.yml` does in Phase 6.

recap: Workflow anatomy: triggers, jobs, steps, runners, `needs`, `if`, `defaults`, `concurrency`.
Reusable workflows with inputs, and an orchestrator workflow that calls them.
Service containers for real integration tests in CI.
Path filters plus an aggregator job for fast and safe required checks.
Caching, artefacts, actionlint, Dependabot and branch protection.

phases.title: Containerise, deliver, and (optionally) deploy to a free tier
phases.heading: Phase 6 · Containerise, deliver and (optionally) deploy
phases.why_md:
A container image is the unit you actually ship: the same bytes run on your laptop, in CI and in
the cloud. In this phase you write a production-grade Dockerfile, run the whole stack with one
command, prove it with a black-box smoke test, and publish versioned images to GitHub Container
Registry (GHCR) automatically on every release tag. Deploying to the cloud is **optional**: everything
graded in this phase works offline on your laptop.
objectives: Write a multi-stage, non-root Dockerfile with a `HEALTHCHECK` for your track.
Add your app to `docker-compose.yml` as a profile and start the stack with `docker compose --profile <track> up`.
Run the language-agnostic smoke test against your container (and against the other tracks' images).
Add a Docker build + smoke job to CI.
Write `deploy.yml`: on a `v*.*.*` tag, build and push images to GHCR; optionally trigger a Render deploy that is **skipped gracefully** when no secret is configured.
Cut release **v1.0.0** with a CHANGELOG entry.

steps.title: The Dockerfile (build context = repository root)
steps.content_md:
All tracks copy the shared migrations into the image, so the build context is the repo root and the
Dockerfile lives in the track: `docker build -f tracks/<track>/Dockerfile .`. Rules:
- **Multi-stage:** compilers and dev dependencies stay in the build stage.
- **Dependencies before source:** copy the manifest, install, then copy `src`, so code changes reuse the dependency layer.
- **Non-root user**, `EXPOSE 8080`, `HEALTHCHECK` hitting `/health`, `MIGRATIONS_DIR=/app/migrations`.

<!-- track:java -->
```dockerfile
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /build
COPY tracks/java/pom.xml tracks/java/checkstyle.xml ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 mvn -B -q dependency:go-offline
COPY tracks/java/src ./src
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 mvn -B -q package -DskipTests -Dcheckstyle.skip -Djacoco.skip=true \
    && java -Djarmode=tools -jar target/app.jar extract --layers --launcher --destination /extracted

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
ENV PORT=8080 MIGRATIONS_DIR=/app/migrations JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75"
WORKDIR /app
RUN useradd --system --uid 10001 app
COPY --from=build /extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build /extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=build /extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build /extracted/application/ ./
COPY spec/db/migrations ./migrations
USER 10001
HEALTHCHECK CMD curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8080/health > /dev/null || exit 1
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"]
```
(abridged; the full file installs `curl` and sets the health-check timings)
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
```dockerfile
FROM python:3.12-slim AS build
WORKDIR /build
COPY tracks/python/requirements.txt .
RUN pip wheel --no-cache-dir --wheel-dir /wheels -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.12-slim
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 PORT=8080 MIGRATIONS_DIR=/app/migrations
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /wheels /wheels
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir /wheels/* && rm -rf /wheels && useradd --system --uid 10001 appuser
COPY tracks/python/app ./app
COPY spec/db/migrations ./migrations
USER 10001
HEALTHCHECK CMD python -c "import urllib.request,sys; sys.exit(0 if urllib.request.urlopen('http://127.0.0.1:8080/health', timeout=2).status == 200 else 1)"
CMD ["python", "-m", "app"]
```
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:typescript -->
```dockerfile
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /build
COPY tracks/typescript/package.json tracks/typescript/package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --no-audit --no-fund
COPY tracks/typescript/tsconfig.json tracks/typescript/tsconfig.build.json ./
COPY tracks/typescript/src ./src
RUN npm run build

FROM node:22-alpine
ENV NODE_ENV=production PORT=8080 MIGRATIONS_DIR=/app/migrations
WORKDIR /app
COPY tracks/typescript/package.json tracks/typescript/package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev --no-audit --no-fund && npm cache clean --force
COPY --from=build /build/dist ./dist
COPY spec/db/migrations ./migrations
USER node
HEALTHCHECK CMD node -e "fetch('http://127.0.0.1:8080/health').then(r=>process.exit(r.ok?0:1)).catch(()=>process.exit(1))"
CMD ["node", "dist/index.js"]
```
<!-- /track -->

The root `.dockerignore` (already in the starter: `**/node_modules`, `**/.venv`, `**/target`, `.git`, …)
keeps the build context small and excludes `.env`, so local secrets never reach the Docker daemon. Build and check the size and user:
```bash

docker image ls snaplink-<track>
docker run --rm --entrypoint id snaplink-<track>:local      # must NOT be uid=0
```

steps.title: Compose profiles: one command for the whole stack
steps.content_md:
Add a service per track to `docker-compose.yml` under a **profile**, sharing one block of environment
variables (a YAML anchor `x-app-env`), `depends_on` with `condition: service_healthy`, and port
`${APP_PORT:-8080}:8080`. Inside Compose the app reaches the database as `postgres:5432`, not `localhost`.
```bash
docker compose --profile <track> up -d --build --wait
docker compose ps
```

steps.title: Smoke test (the same for every track)
steps.content_md:
```bash
scripts/smoke-test.sh                      # default http://localhost:8080
```
It checks 23 behaviours (health, create, alias, 409, 400 problem+json, redirect, click count, stats,
insights, 404, delete) with only `bash` + `curl`. Because the contract is shared, try another track's
image against the same database: `docker compose stop app-<yours>` and `docker compose --profile python up -d`.
Same results. Also run the AI fallback check:
```bash
INSIGHTS_PROVIDER=llm LLM_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:9/v1 docker compose --profile <track> up -d
EXPECT_FALLBACK=true scripts/smoke-test.sh
```

steps.title: CI: build the image and smoke-test it
steps.content_md:
Add a `docker` job (matrix over tracks) to `ci.yml`: `docker/setup-buildx-action`,
`docker/build-push-action` with `load: true` and the GitHub Actions layer cache (`cache-from/to: type=gha`),
then `docker compose --profile <track> up -d --no-build --wait`, the smoke test, logs on failure and `down -v`.

steps.title: Continuous delivery to GHCR: `deploy.yml`
steps.content_md:
Trigger on `push: tags: ["v*.*.*"]`. The job needs `permissions: packages: write` and logs in to
`ghcr.io` with the built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN`; no personal token required. Image names must be lower-case
(the org is `AICanCode-org`), so compute `ghcr.io/${GITHUB_REPOSITORY_OWNER,,}/snaplink-<track>`.
`docker/metadata-action` turns tag `v1.0.0` into image tags `1.0.0`, `1.0`, `sha-<short>` and `latest`.
Read `docs/github-actions-explained.md` §9–§12 for every detail.

steps.title: Release v1.0.0
steps.content_md:
```bash
# update CHANGELOG.md: move "Unreleased" items under "## [1.0.0] - <date>"
git commit -am "chore(release): v1.0.0"
git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "SnapLink v1.0.0"
git push origin main --follow-tags
```
Watch **Actions → Deploy**: three images appear under your profile's **Packages**. New GHCR packages
are **private** by default. Make one public (Package settings → Change visibility) if a host should pull
it without credentials.

steps.title: OPTIONAL: deploy to a free tier
steps.content_md:
You do not need a cloud account to finish this course. If you want a public URL:

| Piece | Free option | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| App | **Render** web service from an *existing image* (`ghcr.io/<you>/snaplink-<track>:latest`) | Free instances sleep when idle; the first request after a pause can take up to a minute (cold start). |
| PostgreSQL | **Neon** free tier | Use its connection string as `DATABASE_URL` and keep `?sslmode=require`. Java: if the string contains `channel_binding=require`, remove that parameter. |
| Redis | **Upstash** free tier (optional) | Use the `rediss://…` (TLS) URL as `REDIS_URL`, or leave `REDIS_URL` unset: SnapLink works without a cache. |
| LLM | none (template), or a free Gemini / Groq key | `INSIGHTS_PROVIDER=llm`, `LLM_BASE_URL`, `LLM_MODEL`, `LLM_API_KEY` as Render env vars. |

Free-tier limits change. Check each provider's pricing page before you rely on it. Fly.io is **not**
used: at the time of writing it needs a payment method and bills usage, with no free tier for new accounts.

To let CI deploy for you:
1. Render → your service → **Settings → Deploy Hook**: copy the URL.
2. GitHub → **Settings → Environments → New environment `production`** (optionally add yourself as a
   required reviewer). Add the **secret** `RENDER_DEPLOY_HOOK_URL` and the **variables** `RENDER_APP_URL`
   (e.g. `https://snaplink-xyz.onrender.com`) and `DEPLOY_TRACK` (`java`, `python` or `typescript`).
3. Push a tag. The `render` job calls the hook with `imgURL=` set to the exact version, waits for
   `/health`, and runs the smoke test against the live URL. Without the secret the job prints a notice
   and **succeeds**, so forks without cloud accounts stay green.

ai_prompts.prompt:
Review this Dockerfile for a <Spring Boot 4 / FastAPI / Fastify> service. Check: multi-stage, layer
caching order, non-root user, HEALTHCHECK, image size, secrets leaking into layers, pinned base image
versions, and anything that would differ between my laptop (amd64/arm64) and CI. <paste Dockerfile>
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: rebuilding and measuring: `docker image ls` (size), `docker run --rm --entrypoint id` (uid), `docker history` (no secrets, small layers), and `docker compose up --wait` (health check passes).

ai_prompts.title: Explain the deploy workflow's security model
ai_prompts.prompt:
In this workflow <paste deploy.yml>, which token pushes to GHCR, what can it do, and for how long?
Is RENDER_DEPLOY_HOOK_URL exposed to pull requests from forks? What would happen if someone pushed a
tag from a fork?
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: reading the GitHub docs pages "Automatic token authentication" and "Using secrets in GitHub Actions" (secrets are not passed to workflows triggered from forks), and checking that `packages: write` appears only on the image job.

ai_prompts.title: Cold start troubleshooting
ai_prompts.prompt:
My container works locally but on Render /health times out for the first minute after idle, then works.
Explain cold starts on free tiers, what my smoke test should do about it, and how to tell a cold start
apart from a crash in the logs.
ai_prompts.verify_by_md: reading your service's Render logs for the boot sequence (migrations applied, listening on port) and timing `curl -w '%{time_total}' $URL/health` after 20 minutes idle.

deliverables.text: `tracks/<track>/Dockerfile` (multi-stage, non-root, HEALTHCHECK).
`docker compose --profile <track> up -d --build --wait` + `scripts/smoke-test.sh`: all checks pass.
CI `docker` job green; `deploy.yml` pushed images to GHCR for tag `v1.0.0`.
`CHANGELOG.md` with `[1.0.0]`; `docs/runbook.md` with start/stop/rollback/rotate-secret steps.
Optional: a live URL in your README and a green `render` job.

quiz.q: Why do the Dockerfiles copy the dependency manifest before the source code?
options: So that the dependency layer is cached and only rebuilt when the manifest changes
quiz.explanation: Layers are cached top-down; anything after a changed layer is rebuilt. Source changes often, dependencies rarely.

quiz.q: Inside Docker Compose, which `DATABASE_URL` host does the app use?
quiz.explanation: Each container has its own `localhost`. Compose gives services DNS names on a shared network.

quiz.q: Why does the image push use `${GITHUB_REPOSITORY_OWNER,,}`?
options: GHCR image names must be lower-case and the org name `AICanCode-org` has capitals
quiz.explanation: `,,` is bash's lower-case expansion. `ghcr.io/AICanCode-org/...` would be rejected.

quiz.q: A fork has no `RENDER_DEPLOY_HOOK_URL` secret. What does the `render` job do on a tag push?
options: Prints a notice and succeeds; the image is still pushed to the fork's GHCR
Waits for someone to add the secret
quiz.explanation: Optional infrastructure must not make the pipeline red. Secrets are read into `env:` and tested with `if: env.X == ''`.

quiz.q: Why are free hosting instances slow on the first request after a while?
options: Idle instances are stopped to save cost and must boot again (cold start)
quiz.explanation: That is why the deploy job polls `/health` for up to 10 minutes before smoke-testing.

recap: Production Dockerfiles: multi-stage, layer caching, non-root, health checks, `.dockerignore`.
Compose profiles to run any track against the same dependencies with one command.
Black-box smoke tests that work for any implementation of a contract.
Image builds with layer caching in CI, and delivery to GHCR with the built-in token on version tags.
Optional, secret-gated deployment that degrades gracefully, plus free-tier trade-offs (cold starts, TLS URLs).
Semantic versioning and a CHANGELOG-driven release.

phases.title: Observability and maintenance
phases.heading: Phase 7 · Observability and maintenance (v1.1.0)
phases.why_md:
Shipping v1.0.0 is the start, not the end. In production you have to answer "is it working right now,
and if not, why?" without attaching a debugger. That needs three things: **logs** you can search,
**metrics** you can graph, and a **request ID** that ties a user's complaint to log lines. Then you
make your first **maintenance change**, a schema migration plus a backward-compatible API field,
and release it safely as v1.1.0.
objectives: Give every request an `X-Request-ID` (reuse a safe incoming one, or generate a UUID) and put it in every log line.
Emit structured **JSON logs**: one object per line, one access-log line per request.
Expose `/metrics` in Prometheus text format with five counters that are identical in every track.
Run a **game day**: stop Redis, observe the metrics and logs, write a short post-mortem.
Ship a backward-compatible change: `V2__add_last_accessed_at.sql` + `lastAccessedAt` in the API, OpenAPI 1.1.0, CHANGELOG, tag `v1.1.0`.
Review and merge one Dependabot PR.

steps.title: Request IDs
steps.content_md:
Rule (shared by all tracks): if the incoming `X-Request-ID` matches `^[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,64}$`, echo it;
otherwise generate a UUID. Never echo arbitrary input: a header containing a newline could inject
fake log lines or headers.

<!-- track:java -->
A `OncePerRequestFilter` (`web/RequestIdFilter.java`) sets the response header, puts `requestId` in
the SLF4J **MDC** (so every log line in that request carries it) and logs one `snaplink.access` line
with `method`, `path`, `status` and `durationMs` using the fluent API
`LOG.atInfo().addKeyValue("status", …).log()`.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
A Starlette `BaseHTTPMiddleware` (`app/observability.py`) stores the ID in `request.state`, sets the
response header and logs one `snaplink.access` record with `extra={"fields": {...}}`.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:typescript -->
Fastify has request IDs built in: `genReqId` (with `requestIdHeader: false`, so we validate the incoming
value ourselves) and a `logController` with `requestIdLogLabel: "requestId"`. An `onSend` hook copies
`request.id` into the `X-Request-ID` response header.
<!-- /track -->

steps.title: `/metrics`
steps.content_md:
Five counters, same names in all tracks (see `GET /metrics` in `spec/openapi.yaml`):
`snaplink_links_created_total`, `snaplink_redirects_total`, `snaplink_cache_hits_total`,
`snaplink_cache_misses_total`, `snaplink_insights_fallback_total`. They are hand-rolled on purpose:
the Prometheus text format is just
```text
# HELP snaplink_redirects_total Successful redirects (302).
# TYPE snaplink_redirects_total counter
snaplink_redirects_total 42
```
In a bigger service you would use Micrometer (Java), `prometheus-client` (Python) or `prom-client` (Node).
Compute the **cache hit ratio** = hits / (hits + misses) after a few redirects.

steps.title: Game day + post-mortem
steps.content_md:
1. Generate traffic: create a link and `for i in $(seq 50); do curl -s -o /dev/null localhost:8080/<code>; done`.
2. `docker compose stop redis`. Redirect 50 more times. What happens to latency, `/health`,
   `cache_misses_total`, and the logs?
3. `docker compose start redis`. Does the hit ratio recover by itself?
4. Write `docs/postmortem-<date>-redis-down.md`: summary, impact, timeline, root cause, what went well,
   what to improve, action items. Blameless: describe systems, not people.
5. The reference solution automates steps 1–3 in `scripts/game-day.sh <track>`
   (`git show phase-7-end:scripts/game-day.sh`). Its post-mortem found a real problem in one track:
   read it **after** writing yours (`git show phase-7-end:docs/postmortem-2026-10-02-redis-down.md`).

steps.title: Maintenance change: `lastAccessedAt` (v1.1.0)
steps.content_md:
1. `spec/db/migrations/V2__add_last_accessed_at.sql`: `ALTER TABLE links ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS
   last_accessed_at TIMESTAMPTZ NULL;` Nullable, no default rewrite, so old code keeps working.
2. The click statement also sets `last_accessed_at` (the repository now receives the full timestamp,
   not just the day).
3. The `Link` JSON gains an **optional** `lastAccessedAt` (null until the first click). Adding a field is
   backward compatible; removing or renaming one is not.
4. `spec/openapi.yaml` → `version: 1.1.0`; `CHANGELOG.md` → `## [1.1.0]`; bump the track's version.
5. Tests first: an API test with the fake clock (`lastAccessedAt` = the time of the click) and an
   integration test that the column is filled.
6. Release: `git tag -a v1.1.0 -m "SnapLink v1.1.0" && git push origin main --follow-tags`.
   `deploy.yml` publishes `:1.1.0` and moves `:latest`.

quiz.q: Why validate an incoming `X-Request-ID` before echoing it?
options: An unvalidated value could inject newlines or fake fields into logs and headers
quiz.explanation: Treat every header as untrusted input. A strict allow-list regex is the simplest defence.

quiz.q: Which metric tells you Redis is down even when `/health` was not checked?
quiz.explanation: Redirects keep working (from Postgres), so the symptom is a falling hit ratio, which is exactly why you graph it.

quiz.q: Why is `ADD COLUMN … NULL` (no default, not `NOT NULL`) the safe choice?
options: Postgres does not support `NOT NULL` columns
Old app versions that do not know the column keep working, and the change is instant
quiz.explanation: Expand first, (optionally) contract later. A `NOT NULL` column would break inserts from v1.0.0 during a rolling deploy.

quiz.q: Adding `lastAccessedAt` to the response is a … change.
quiz.explanation: SemVer: new optional fields are minor. Removing or renaming a field would be major (2.0.0).

quiz.q: What makes a post-mortem "blameless"?
options: It focuses on how the system and process allowed the failure, not on who made a mistake
quiz.explanation: People hide problems when they fear blame. Blameless reviews produce better action items.

recap: Correlation IDs, MDC/context propagation and structured JSON logs.
Prometheus counters, the text exposition format and the cache hit ratio.
Game days and blameless post-mortems.
Expand-style, backward-compatible migrations and SemVer minor releases.
Dependency maintenance with Dependabot, and the role of CI as the safety net.

phases.heading: Phase 8 · Retrospective and portfolio
phases.why_md:
A recruiter spends about a minute on your repository. A README that tells the story (problem,
design, trade-offs, evidence, what you would do next) turns "another URL shortener" into proof that
you can design, test, ship and operate software, and that you use AI responsibly. The retrospective
is for you: it turns nine phases of experience into lessons you can explain in an interview.
objectives: Rewrite the README top section as a **case study** with real numbers from your project.
Write a short **retrospective** (what went well, what didn't, what you'd change).
Summarise your **AI_LOG** into three honest bullet points.
Prepare a 2-minute walkthrough and answers to common interview questions about the project.

steps.content_md:

```bash
git log --oneline | wc -l                       # commits
git tag -l 'v*'                                  # releases
make coverage                                    # coverage % per track
scripts/smoke-test.sh | tail -1                  # e.g. "27 passed, 0 failed"
curl -s localhost:8080/metrics | grep _total     # metrics after a demo session
```
Also grab: a screenshot of the CI run graph, the GHCR package page and (optionally) your live URL.

steps.title: README case study
steps.content_md:
At the top of `README.md`, before the setup instructions, add a section with:
1. **One-line pitch** and a demo GIF or `curl` session.
2. **Problem → solution** in three sentences.
3. **Architecture** (link the Mermaid diagram) and the **three decisions** you are proudest of, linking ADRs.
4. **Quality evidence:** tests, coverage, CI badge, smoke test, failure tests (Redis down).
5. **Operations:** health, metrics, request IDs, the post-mortem.
6. **How I used AI**, with honest examples of accepted and rejected suggestions.
7. **What I'd do next** (rate limiting, a dashboard UI, k6 load test, OpenTelemetry tracing…).

steps.title: Retrospective (`docs/retrospective.md`)
steps.content_md:
Use *Start / Stop / Continue* or *What went well / What didn't / What I'd change*. Include one
technical lesson (e.g. cache TTL must respect expiry), one process lesson (test-first with a pending
list), and one AI lesson (an assistant confidently produced a wrong answer and a test caught it).

steps.title: Practise the walkthrough
steps.content_md:
Record yourself (2 minutes): problem, architecture diagram, one interesting piece of code, the test
that proves it, the CI run, what you'd do next. Then answer out loud:
- *Why 302 and not 301?* · *What happens when Redis is down?* · *How do you avoid duplicate codes?*
- *How do you know your tests are good, not just numerous?* · *Where did AI help, and where did it mislead you?*

steps.content_md:

`docker`, `github-actions`, and post the case study (aicancode.org *Build in public*, LinkedIn).

steps.title: Phase 0 · Setup and orientation
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
Every professional project starts with a working local environment and a clean Git workflow. Teams
lose days to "works on my machine". In this phase you set up the tools for **one** track, run the
starter, open your first pull request and start your `AI_LOG.md`. That is the evidence a reviewer
looks for first: a repo that builds from a clean checkout with one command.

## 2. Objectives
By the end of this phase you can:
- Fork the repository **with all branches and tags**, clone it and add the `upstream` remote.
- Pick a track (Java, Python or TypeScript) and install its toolchain on Windows (WSL2), macOS or Linux.
- Start PostgreSQL + Redis with Docker Compose and run the starter so `GET /health` returns `UP`.
- Run lint and tests locally and see which tests are *pending* and why.
- Open a pull request that passes CI and write your first `AI_LOG.md` entry.

## 3. Step-by-step instructions

### Step 0.1 · Fork and clone (keep the tags!)
1. On GitHub open `AICanCode-org/snaplink` → **Fork**. **Untick "Copy the `main` branch only"**. The
   `solution` branch and the `phase-N-end` tags are your safety net in later phases.
2. Clone **your** fork and connect the original as `upstream`:
   ```bash
   git clone https://github.com/<you>/snaplink.git
   cd snaplink
   git remote add upstream https://github.com/AICanCode-org/snaplink.git
   git fetch upstream --tags
   git tag -l 'phase-*'      # you should see phase-0-end … phase-8-end
   ```
3. **Windows:** do all of this inside **WSL2** (Ubuntu) and keep the repo in the Linux file system
   (`~/code/snaplink`), not under `/mnt/c`. File watching and Docker volumes are 5–10× faster there.

### Step 0.2 · Install Docker and the tools for ONE track
* **All tracks:** Git, Docker (Docker Desktop on Windows/macOS with the WSL2 backend; Docker Engine +
  compose plugin on Linux), `make` and `curl`.
* Then run the doctor script. It tells you exactly what is missing:
  ```bash
  scripts/doctor.sh
  ```

<!-- track:java -->
**Java track:** JDK 21 (Temurin) and Maven 3.9+. The easiest way on Linux/macOS/WSL is SDKMAN:
```bash
curl -s https://get.sdkman.io | bash   # then open a new terminal
sdk install java 21-tem && sdk install maven
java -version && mvn -v
```
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
**Python track:** Python 3.11+ with `venv` (Ubuntu/WSL: `sudo apt install python3 python3-venv`;
macOS: `brew install python@3.12`).
```bash
python3 --version
cd tracks/python && make install     # creates .venv and installs pinned dependencies
```
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:typescript -->
**TypeScript track:** Node.js 20+ (22 LTS recommended). Install it with nvm:
```bash
curl -o- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nvm-sh/nvm/v0.40.1/install.sh | bash   # new terminal
nvm install 22 && node -v
cd tracks/typescript && make install   # npm ci
```
<!-- /track -->

### Step 0.3 · Start the infrastructure
```bash
docker compose up -d postgres redis
docker compose ps          # both should be "healthy"
```
The first start also creates a second database, `snaplink_test`, that the integration tests use
(`spec/db/init/01-create-test-db.sql`), so tests can never wipe your dev data.

### Step 0.4 · Run the starter
<!-- track:java -->
```bash
cd tracks/java
make run                   # mvn spring-boot:run, listens on :8080
```
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
```bash
cd tracks/python
make run                   # python -m app (uvicorn), listens on :8080
```
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:typescript -->
```bash
cd tracks/typescript
make run                   # tsx watch src/index.ts, listens on :8080
```
<!-- /track -->

In another terminal:
```bash
curl -s localhost:8080/health
# {"status":"UP","checks":{"database":"UP","cache":"UP"}}
```
The link endpoints already exist but answer `500` because the business logic is a `TODO` — that is
Phase 3. Stop Redis (`docker compose stop redis`) and call `/health` again: `cache` becomes `DOWN` but
the status stays `UP`. Start it again with `docker compose start redis`.

### Step 0.5 · Run the checks and meet the pending tests
```bash
make lint test
```
You will see **one passing test** (`/health`) and dozens of **skipped** ones. They are *pending*: the
complete test suite for SnapLink is already written and switched off in one file per track:

| Track | Pending list |
|---|---|
| Java | `tracks/java/src/test/java/org/aicancode/snaplink/support/Pending.java` |
| Python | `tracks/python/tests/conftest.py` (`PENDING`) |
| TypeScript | `tracks/typescript/test/pending.ts` (`PENDING`) |

In Phase 3 you delete one line at a time, watch the tests go red, and make them green.

### Step 0.6 · Your first pull request
1. Create a branch: `git switch -c chore/phase-0-setup`.
2. Fill in the first entry in `AI_LOG.md`, e.g. how an assistant helped you install the toolchain and
   how you checked its advice.
3. Commit and push, then open a PR **in your fork** against your `main`:
   ```bash
   git add AI_LOG.md
   git commit -m "docs: start AI_LOG for phase 0"
   git push -u origin chore/phase-0-setup
   ```
4. Open the **Actions** tab: the CI workflow runs lint + unit tests for all three tracks. Wait for green,
   fill in the PR template and merge.

## 4. AI-assist prompts

### Prompt 1: Fix my toolchain install
```text
I'm on <Windows 11 + WSL2 Ubuntu 24.04 | macOS 15 | Ubuntu 24.04>. I want to run a <Java 21 + Maven |
Python 3.12 | Node 22> project with Docker Compose. Here is the output of scripts/doctor.sh:
<paste output>. Give me the exact commands to install what is missing, explain each one in one line,
and tell me how to verify each install.
```
**Verify the output by:** running each verification command it gives you, re-running
`scripts/doctor.sh` until every line is green, and checking any download URL against the official site
(adoptium.net, python.org, nodejs.org, docker.com). Never pipe an unknown URL into `bash`.

### Prompt 2: Explain the starter
```text
Here is the file tree of a starter project and the file <tracks/<track>/…/main entry file>:
<paste>. Explain in plain English what happens from "make run" until GET /health returns, which
files are involved, and where environment variables are read. Do not suggest code changes.
```
**Verify the output by:** setting a breakpoint or a log line where it says the config is read, and
changing `PORT=8081 make run` to confirm the app really listens on the new port.

## 5. Deliverables
- [ ] Your fork contains the `solution` branch and the `phase-*` tags (`git tag -l` shows them).
- [ ] `docker compose up -d postgres redis` works; `GET /health` returns `UP` from your track.
- [ ] `make lint test` passes locally (1 passed, the rest skipped).
- [ ] A merged PR with a green CI run.
- [ ] `AI_LOG.md` has its first entry.

## 6. Self-check quiz

### Q1. Why must you untick "Copy the main branch only" when forking?
- [ ] Otherwise GitHub Actions is disabled in the fork
- [x] Otherwise the `solution` branch and phase tags are missing from your fork
- [ ] Otherwise you cannot open pull requests
- [ ] Otherwise Docker Compose cannot find the database
> **Answer:** Forks copy only `main` by default. The tags (`phase-N-end`) live on the `solution` branch;
> without them you cannot compare your work or catch up. Fix it later with `git fetch upstream --tags`.

### Q2. On Windows, where should the repository live?
- [ ] `C:\Users\you\snaplink`, opened from WSL as `/mnt/c/Users/you/snaplink`
- [x] Inside the WSL2 Linux file system, e.g. `~/code/snaplink`
- [ ] On a network drive so Docker can share it
- [ ] It does not matter
> **Answer:** Cross-file-system access from WSL to `/mnt/c` is slow and breaks file watching. Keep code in
> the Linux file system and open it with VS Code's WSL extension.

### Q3. `/health` says `"cache":"DOWN"` but `"status":"UP"`. What does that mean?
- [ ] The app is broken and should be restarted
- [x] Redis is unavailable, but the app can still serve requests from PostgreSQL
- [ ] PostgreSQL is down
- [ ] The health endpoint has a bug
> **Answer:** Redis is an optional cache (NFR-2). Only the database is required for `UP`; without it the
> endpoint returns `503`.

### Q4. Why are most tests skipped in the starter?
- [ ] They are flaky
- [ ] CI is too slow to run them
- [x] They describe behaviour you will implement in Phase 3–4 and are switched on one milestone at a time
- [ ] They only run on the solution branch
> **Answer:** The full suite is written up-front (a test-first workflow). Deleting a line from the pending
> list turns a group back on, so you always have a clear red → green target.

### Q5. Which of these should never go into an AI prompt?
- [ ] The output of `scripts/doctor.sh`
- [ ] A stack trace from your own code
- [x] The contents of your `.env` file with API keys
- [ ] The OpenAPI spec
> **Answer:** Secrets and personal data never go into prompts. Redact keys before you paste anything.

## 7. What you learned
- A reproducible local environment: Docker Compose for dependencies, one toolchain per track.
- The difference between `origin` (your fork) and `upstream` (the course repo), and why tags matter.
- How a health check reports dependencies, and that an optional cache must not take the app down.
- Pending tests as a to-do list: the spec is executable before you write any code.
- The PR + CI loop and the habit of logging AI assistance.

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
# Start Phase 1 from the reference end of Phase 0:
git switch -c my-phase-1 phase-0-end
# See what the reference changed in this phase:
git diff main phase-0-end --stat
```

steps.title: Phase 1 · Requirements and user stories
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
Most failed projects fail before the first line of code: nobody wrote down what "done" means. A short,
testable requirements document lets you say *no* to scope creep, gives every test a reason to exist,
and is the first thing an interviewer asks about ("what were the constraints?"). AI assistants are
great at drafting requirements, and just as good at inventing requirements nobody asked for. Your
job is to keep the ones you can test.

## 2. Objectives
- Turn a one-paragraph brief into numbered **functional** (FR) and **measurable non-functional** (NFR) requirements.
- Write 6–8 **user stories** with Given/When/Then acceptance criteria and create them as GitHub Issues.
- Write an explicit **out-of-scope** list.
- Do a **back-of-the-envelope estimate** (traffic, storage, collision probability) and use it to justify the design.

## 3. Step-by-step instructions

### Step 1.1 · Read the brief and the contract
> *Build SnapLink: a self-hostable URL shortener. Users create short links (random or custom alias,
> optional expiry), visitors are redirected, owners see daily click counts and a short weekly insight.
> It must run on a laptop for free, keep working when the cache is down, and store no personal data.*

Open `spec/openapi.yaml`. The HTTP contract is **given** so the three tracks stay compatible; your
requirements must be consistent with it (status codes, limits, error format).

### Step 1.2 · Functional requirements
In `spec/requirements.md` write FR-1 … FR-n as "The system shall …" statements. Each needs a number
(1–365 days, 2048 characters, 3–32 alias characters) or a status code, so a test can check it.
Bad: *"Links should be short."* Good: *"Codes are 7 Base62 characters."*

### Step 1.3 · Non-functional requirements
Cover performance, availability, security, privacy, cost and portability. Make each one measurable:
*"p95 redirect latency < 50 ms with a warm cache"*, *"redirects keep working when Redis is down"*,
*"no IP addresses are stored"*.

### Step 1.4 · User stories → GitHub Issues
For each story use the **User story** issue template (`.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/user_story.yml`). It asks
for the story, the acceptance criteria and the Phase 3 milestone. Label them `user-story`. With the
GitHub CLI:
```bash
gh issue create --template user_story.yml      # or use the web UI: Issues → New issue
```

### Step 1.5 · Out of scope + estimates
List what v1 will **not** do (accounts, UI dashboard, QR codes, rate limiting…). Then estimate:
links/day, read:write ratio, requests/second at peak (× 10 of average), storage per year, and the
chance that a random 7-character code collides. Write one sentence on what the numbers mean for the design.

### Step 1.6 · Commit
```bash
git switch -c docs/phase-1-requirements
git add spec/requirements.md AI_LOG.md
git commit -m "docs(spec): requirements, user stories and estimates"
git push -u origin docs/phase-1-requirements     # open a PR, merge when CI is green
```
The track code does not change in this phase, so `make lint test` behaves exactly as in Phase 0.

## 4. AI-assist prompts

### Prompt 1: Draft requirements from the brief
```text
Act as a senior engineer. From this brief, write numbered functional requirements (FR-n, "The system
shall ...") and measurable non-functional requirements (NFR-n) for a URL shortener. Every requirement
must be testable: include numbers, limits or HTTP status codes. Stay consistent with this OpenAPI
contract: <paste the paths + schemas of spec/openapi.yaml>. Brief: <paste>. Do NOT add features that
are not in the brief; list anything you were tempted to add under "Out of scope".
```
**Verify the output by:** checking every FR against `spec/openapi.yaml` (same limits, same status codes),
deleting anything you cannot write a test for, and moving invented features (accounts, QR codes,
analytics by country) to *Out of scope*.

### Prompt 2: Acceptance criteria review
```text
Here are my user stories with acceptance criteria: <paste>. For each story, list (a) criteria that are
ambiguous or not testable, (b) a missing edge case, (c) the HTTP request + expected response that
would prove the criterion. Answer as a table.
```
**Verify the output by:** turning at least two of the suggested request/response pairs into `curl`
commands you will run in Phase 3, and rejecting edge cases that contradict the contract.

### Prompt 3: Check my estimate
```text
I estimate 1,000 new links/day and a 100:1 read:write ratio. Check my arithmetic for average and peak
requests per second, yearly storage at 0.5 KB per row, and the probability that a new random
7-character Base62 code collides when 1 million codes exist. Show each calculation step.
```
**Verify the output by:** redoing the arithmetic yourself (62⁷ ≈ 3.52 × 10¹²; 100,000 / 86,400 ≈ 1.16 req/s).
LLMs make arithmetic slips; a calculator does not.

## 5. Deliverables
- [ ] `spec/requirements.md` with FRs, measurable NFRs, ≥ 6 user stories with acceptance criteria, out of scope, estimates.
- [ ] One GitHub Issue per user story, labelled `user-story`, each assigned to a Phase 3 milestone.
- [ ] An `AI_LOG.md` entry that records at least one AI suggestion you **rejected** and why.
- [ ] Compare with the reference: `git diff phase-0-end phase-1-end -- spec/requirements.md`.

## 6. Self-check quiz

### Q1. Which requirement is testable?
- [ ] "Redirects should be fast."
- [ ] "The system should be secure."
- [x] "p95 server-side redirect latency is below 50 ms with a warm cache."
- [ ] "Users should love the aliases."
> **Answer:** Only the third one has a measurable threshold and a condition. The others need numbers before they can be tested.

### Q2. Why does SnapLink use `302` instead of `301` (and why is that a requirement, not just a detail)?
- [ ] `302` is faster
- [x] Browsers cache `301` permanently, which would break expiry, deletion and click counting
- [ ] `301` is deprecated
- [ ] Search engines require `302`
> **Answer:** FR-3, FR-5 and FR-6 only work if every click reaches the server. That constraint leads to ADR-0002 in Phase 2.

### Q3. With 1 million existing random 7-character Base62 codes, the chance that a new code collides is about…
- [ ] 1 in 62
- [ ] 1 in 1,000
- [x] 3 in 10 million
- [ ] Zero, codes are unique by construction
> **Answer:** 10⁶ / 62⁷ ≈ 10⁶ / 3.5 × 10¹² ≈ 2.8 × 10⁻⁷. That is rare, but not zero, so the database must still enforce uniqueness and the app retries.

### Q4. What belongs in "Out of scope"?
- [ ] Requirements you could not finish
- [x] Features you deliberately will not build in this version, so reviewers know it was a decision
- [ ] Bugs
- [ ] Non-functional requirements
> **Answer:** Writing the list down stops scope creep and shows judgement. "No accounts in v1" is a decision, not an omission.

### Q5. "Redirects keep working when Redis is down" is an example of…
- [ ] A functional requirement
- [x] An availability NFR that will become an integration test
- [ ] A user story
- [ ] An implementation detail you should not write down
> **Answer:** It is about *how well* the system behaves under failure. Phase 4 proves it with a test that points the cache at a dead port.

## 7. What you learned
- How to turn a fuzzy brief into numbered, testable FRs and measurable NFRs.
- User stories with Given/When/Then criteria, tracked as GitHub Issues.
- Why an explicit out-of-scope list is a professional signal.
- Back-of-the-envelope estimation and how it justifies (or rules out) complexity.
- Using AI to draft, and your own judgement and arithmetic to verify.

## 8. Catch-up git commands
```bash
git fetch upstream --tags
git switch -c my-phase-2 phase-1-end           # continue from the reference requirements
git show phase-1-end:spec/requirements.md | less
git diff phase-0-end phase-1-end --stat
```

steps.title: Phase 2 · Design: architecture, database schema, API contract
steps.content:
## 1. Why it matters
Design is where you make the expensive decisions on purpose: how codes are generated, what is cached,
where the source of truth lives, what happens when something fails. Writing them down as diagrams
and **Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)** lets a reviewer follow your reasoning in minutes, and
lets future-you remember *why*. The SQL schema is the one artefact that is shared by all three
tracks, so a mistake here costs three times.

## 2. Objectives
- Draw context, container and sequence diagrams in Mermaid (rendered by GitHub).
- Write three ADRs: short-code generation, redirect status code, click counting.
- Design the PostgreSQL schema and write it as migration `spec/db/migrations/V1__init.sql`.
- Read the given OpenAPI contract and map each endpoint to a requirement.
- Watch your track's migrator apply V1 on start-up.

## 3. Step-by-step instructions

### Step 2.1 · Diagrams in `spec/architecture.md`
Mermaid is text, so it diffs and reviews like code. Start with a container diagram:
```text
flowchart TB
    client([HTTP clients]) --> app["SnapLink app :8080"]
    app -- "SQL (source of truth)" --> pg[("PostgreSQL")]
    app -- "cache-aside, 500 ms timeout" --> redis[("Redis")]
    app -. "optional, falls back to template" .-> llm[("LLM endpoint")]
```
Wrap it in a code fence with the language `mermaid` and preview it on GitHub or in VS Code (extension
"Markdown Preview Mermaid Support"). Then draw the **redirect sequence**: cache hit, cache miss,
unknown code, expired link, and Redis down.

### Step 2.2 · ADRs
Copy `spec/adr/0000-template.md` three times:
1. `0001-short-code-generation.md`: sequence + Base62 vs hash vs random CSPRNG + retry. Use your Phase 1 collision estimate.
2. `0002-302-redirects.md`: `301` vs `302` vs `307`, and what browser caching does to analytics.
3. `0003-click-counting.md`: two statements vs one atomic statement vs Redis `INCR` + periodic flush.

Each ADR is one page: context, options with pros/cons, decision, consequences.

### Step 2.3 · Schema → `spec/db/migrations/V1__init.sql`
Requirements to satisfy:
- `links`: surrogate `BIGSERIAL` id, unique `code` (≤ 32 chars), `long_url` ≤ 2048 enforced by a
  `CHECK`, `is_custom`, `created_at`, nullable `expires_at`, `click_count`.
- A **partial index** on `expires_at` for rows that can expire.
- `click_daily(link_id, day, clicks)` with a composite primary key and `ON DELETE CASCADE`.

Name the unique constraint (`uq_links_code`) so that error messages and tests can refer to it. Never
edit a migration after it is merged. Add `V2__…` instead (you will do that in Phase 7).

### Step 2.4 · Watch the migrator apply it
Every track runs the same tiny migrator at start-up (≈ 40 lines, no Flyway/Alembic, so the three tracks
can share one SQL file). Start your app (`make run`) and inspect the result:
```bash
docker compose exec postgres psql -U snaplink -d snaplink -c '\d links' -c 'select * from schema_migrations'
```

<!-- track:java -->
Java: `tracks/java/src/main/java/org/aicancode/snaplink/db/Migrator.java`, called from the `migrator`
bean in `config/AppConfig.java`. The `linkRepository` bean depends on it, so Spring cannot serve
traffic against an old schema.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:python -->
Python: `tracks/python/app/db.py` → `run_migrations()`, called in the FastAPI `lifespan` in `app/main.py`.
<!-- /track -->

<!-- track:typescript -->
TypeScript: `tracks/typescript/src/db.ts` → `runMigrations()`, awaited in `src/index.ts` before `listen()`.
<!-- /track -->

### Step 2.5 · Map the contract
For every path in `spec/openapi.yaml`, write the FR number next to it (in a table in
`architecture.md` or as a comment in your notes). Any endpoint without a requirement, or any
requirement without an endpoint, is a design bug: fix one of the two. Validate the file:
```bash
pipx run openapi-spec-validator spec/openapi.yaml       # or: npx @redocly/cli lint spec/openapi.yaml
```

### Step 2.6 · Commit
```bash
git switch -c docs/phase-2-design
git add spec/
git commit -m "docs(spec): architecture, ADRs 0001-0003, V1 schema"
```

## 4. AI-assist prompts

### Prompt 1: Mermaid sequence diagram
```text
Write a Mermaid sequenceDiagram for GET /{code} in a URL shortener with participants Browser, App,
Redis, Postgres. Use alt blocks for: cache hit, cache miss, unknown code (404), expired link (410,
also delete the cache key), and Redis timeout (treated as a miss). Clicks are recorded with one SQL
statement after the expiry check, and a failure to record must not break the redirect.
```
**Verify the output by:** pasting it into https://mermaid.live (it must render without errors) and
walking through each `alt` branch against FR-3, FR-4, FR-5 and NFR-2 in your requirements.

### Prompt 2: Review my schema
```text
Review this PostgreSQL 16 migration for a URL shortener: <paste V1__init.sql>. Requirements: <paste
FR-1..FR-7>. Point out missing constraints, wrong types, missing or useless indexes, and anything that
would make "delete a link and its analytics" or "count a click atomically" hard. Do not add tables for
features that are out of scope.
```
**Verify the output by:** running the migration (`make run`, then `\d links`) and trying the failure
cases by hand in `psql`: insert a duplicate code (must fail with `uq_links_code`), a 3,000-character URL
(must fail the CHECK), delete a link that has `click_daily` rows (they must disappear).

### Prompt 3: Steel-man the option I rejected
```text
For a URL shortener with ~12 requests/second at peak, argue as convincingly as you can FOR counting
clicks with Redis INCR and a periodic flush to Postgres, then list the failure modes. Keep it under
200 words.
```
**Verify the output by:** checking each claimed failure mode against your architecture (what happens on
a crash between flushes? when Redis is down?), and record the decision and the trade-off in ADR-0003.

## 5. Deliverables
- [ ] `spec/architecture.md` with context, container, redirect-sequence and ER diagrams that render on GitHub.
- [ ] `spec/adr/0001…0003` accepted.
- [ ] `spec/db/migrations/V1__init.sql`; the app applies it on start-up (`schema_migrations` has version 1).
- [ ] Every OpenAPI path mapped to a requirement.
- [ ] Compare: `git diff phase-1-end phase-2-end --stat`.

## 6. Self-check quiz

### Q1. Why is uniqueness of `code` enforced by a database constraint instead of "SELECT first, then INSERT"?
- [ ] SELECTs are slow
- [x] Two concurrent requests can both see "free" and both insert. Only the constraint is race-free
- [ ] The ORM requires it
- [ ] Constraints use less disk space
> **Answer:** Check-then-act is a race. Insert, catch the unique violation, and retry (random code) or return `409` (custom alias).

### Q2. What does the partial index `… WHERE expires_at IS NOT NULL` buy us?
- [x] An index only over rows that can expire, so it stays small
- [ ] It makes the column nullable
- [ ] It deletes expired rows automatically
- [ ] It speeds up redirects by code
